body: Clack, clack, clack, the length of a mile. The lounge TV has CNN on a replay from Berlin, where it’s already six o’clock tomorrow morning: a line of painted slabs taller than a man, standing in a lit street along the route where the Wall used to run, and at the head of the line an old man in a dark coat puts out one hand and pushes. LECH WALESA, says the caption. The dominoes go away from him in a long curve toward the lights of the Brandenburg Gate, each one taking down the next, past the cameras and out of the frame.

Margot has the whiteboard. Under her headline she has ruled four columns and labeled them in square capitals: GORBACHEV, her own, because a man declining to send the tanks “is the most underrated political act of the twentieth century, and I’m including penicillin”; THE POPE, for Costigan; A UNION, for Broussard; and HASSELHOFF, for Theo, who is lying on the carpet with his feet up the wall.

“New Year’s Eve, 1989,” Theo tells the ceiling. “A cherry picker. A leather jacket wired with lights. A scarf made of piano keys. He sang ‘Looking for Freedom’ to half a million Germans and the Wall took the hint. I’d option it.”

Laney, cross-legged in the good armchair with a bag of Kettle chips, says, “The Germans, sugar. They did it with their *hands*.” Margot writes THE GERMANS (PRICE) small in the corner, as a concession to democracy. Kevin has the stopwatch going on his BlackBerry and has announced three-minute openings, “and I will cut you off, I did Model UN.” Doug Pruitt is asleep on the couch under the lost-and-found afghan and has been since the Steelers’ second quarter. Becca is in Portolá with a lab report due at eight; her text said *have fun!! argue nice!!*

body.text: The Newman stockpot sits on the lounge counter with Lena’s court-bouillon in it, waiting on the Harbor Inn’s night shift: Saturday’s rockfish, out of Rudy’s walk-in this afternoon, the masking tape that said LENA’S. MONDAY. FOR THE HARBOR INN. now stuck to the pot handle. She ladles Jack a bowl before anybody starts and puts it in his hands. “Eat. I don’t beat a man on an empty stomach. It isn’t sporting.”

There’s no pot tonight. Lena has the other armchair, her boots on the coffee table and a mug of tea going cold on her knee, and in her cardigan pocket, folded small with one corner showing, the Anchor napkin from Saturday’s wedding. Nobody mentions it, Jack least of all.

body: “Twenty years ago tonight,” Margot says, “a Party spokesman in East Berlin read out a memo on live television that he hadn’t finished reading, and a city walked through a wall. Tonight we assign credit. Professor Hale isn’t here, so it doesn’t count, so you’ll all be honest.” She points the marker. “Broussard. Three minutes.”
Lena doesn’t get up. She doesn’t need to.

“August 1980,” she says. “An electrician who’d been fired from the Lenin Shipyard climbs the fence to get back *in* — in, Costigan, he climbed in — and by the end of the month the government has signed for a free union. Welders. Crane operators. Women from the canteen. Ten million people out of a country of thirty-five. They declared martial law to kill it, and it outlived them.” She nods at the TV, where the old man in the dark coat is still pushing his domino, in slow motion now, from a second angle. “The only mass movement anywhere behind the Iron Curtain was a labor union. The Pope said *Be not afraid*, and the people who heard him were holding welding torches. And who do they get to push the first domino tonight? Not a cardinal. An electrician.”
“Two fifty-one,” says Kevin.

choices.text: “There was an altar at every gate in Gdańsk. They said Mass at the strike. The union was the Church in overalls.”
response: “The altar I’ll give you.” Lena holds up a finger. “I’ve seen the pictures — Mass at Gate Two, the Black Madonna wired to the fence, priests hearing confessions on folding chairs.” A second finger. “But the *overalls*, Costigan. The overalls are mine. You just agreed with me in Latin.”
Margot writes ALTAR (CONCEDED) under A UNION, and then, after some thought, OVERALLS (DISPUTED).

choices.text: “He climbed a wall to get in. Ten years later everybody climbed one to get out. Trendsetter.”
response: The lounge goes up. Theo repeats *trendsetter* reverently to the ceiling, and Laney throws a Kettle chip at Jack on principle, and Doug says “What” in his sleep and goes back under.
Lena laughs — one loud bark out of her, the kind she would never own to — and points across the coffee table at him. “That was cheap,” she says, “and I hate that it worked.”

choices.text: “Welders and electricians. My father would’ve joined it in a day.”
response: “I know he would,” Lena says, and she’s glad of it; it’s all over her. “I’d have marched behind him with a sign.”
She looks at Jack the way she does when he gives her anything about home, as if she means to keep it, and then she goes on, faster.

choices.text: “Leipzig. Prayers for peace at the Nikolaikirche every Monday at five. October ninth, seventy thousand in the street with candles — so their hands were full.”
response: “— and nobody could say they were carrying anything else,” Lena finishes for him. She knows it too: you need both hands for a candle, one to hold it and one to keep the wind off.
She looks at him like he’s gone into her pocket and come out with her best line. Margot writes LEIPZIG under THE POPE without a word.

body: The TV runs the dominoes again from a helicopter, and from up there the whole line goes over like a zipper coming undone down the middle of Berlin. Doug turns over under the afghan. Laney has finished the Kettle chips and is reading the bag. Margot caps the marker, uncaps it, and says, “Broussard. Your second, or your rebuttal, or whatever you people call it.”
Lena gets up for this one. She goes to the window, where Berlin isn’t, and turns around with her back to the Lagoon.

“So it falls,” she says. “On a Thursday. And by Saturday they’re lined up around the block outside the grocery stores in West Berlin to buy *bananas*. The West shows up with blue jeans and a McDonald’s and buys what’s left of the East for a mark apiece. You want to know who won the Cold War, Margot? Not Gorbachev. Not the Pope. The *mall*.” She finds Jack. “Twenty years later — ask your daddy who won. GM took a bailout and he took a pink slip. That’s the market that won, Jack. Same one.”

It’s a good argument. It’s the argument she makes about her father’s shrimpers and the insurance men, with Frank in it instead, because Jack told her about Frank himself, back in September. She holds his eye the entire time she makes it.
“Two minutes even,” Kevin says.

choices.text: “The market didn’t build the Wall. It just never needed one.”
response: Lena tips her head to him, a fencer touched, and doesn’t give up an inch of the strip. “It never needed a wall,” she says. “It had a mortgage.” But Margot has already written NEVER NEEDED ONE under THE POPE, and underlined *needed*, and Lena watches her do it and doesn’t argue.

choices.text: “He’d tell you GM lost. Then he’d tell you the Browns lost worse.”
choices.key: Monday night Lena said your father’s pink slip was the market that won. You gave her the point.
response: Lena softens. He watches it happen from the mouth up.
“Tell him I said the Browns are a structural problem,” she says. “Tell him I said it with love.”
From the armchair, very quietly, Laney says, “Aw.”

choices.key: Monday night Lena brought your father into the argument. You told her to leave him out of it.
response: It wins the room. “*Ooh*,” Theo says from the carpet, with real appreciation, and Margot’s marker stops halfway down a letter.
Lena looks at Jack across the coffee table. Whatever she thinks of it, she keeps.
“All right,” she says, level, and she leaves him out of it.

choices.text: “Sindermann. The regime’s own man: *We had planned for everything. We were prepared for everything. Except candles and prayers.*”
response: “Source?” says Margot.
“He said it on his deathbed.”
“*Source.*”
“Everybody quotes it.”

“Everybody quotes Einstein on insanity,” Margot says. “He never said that either.” But she writes CANDLES & PRAYERS (ALLEGEDLY) under THE POPE, and Lena, who looked ready to go after the attribution herself, lets Margot do it for her and grins at the carpet.

body: She makes her third move sitting down, on the arm of the couch by Doug’s feet, with her hand at her collar turning the medal on its chain while she thinks.

body.text: There is no Frank in it anywhere. She builds it around the place where he would have gone.

body: “June of ’79,” Lena says. “He goes home to Warsaw for the first time as Pope and says Mass in Victory Square in front of the Party and everybody, and he prays — *Let your Spirit descend, and renew the face of the earth* —” she stops where he stopped, “— *the face of this land*. And the square won’t let him go on.” She lets go of the medal. “Candles in Leipzig. A union in Gdańsk. And a Polish pope who was both. You want it to be prayer *instead of* bread, Jack. It was prayer *and* bread. That’s the whole Church, and you keep picking one.”
Kevin says, “Time,” softly, to his BlackBerry, and doesn’t press it.

journal.title: On the Wall
journal.text: On the Wall — unofficial, Margot’s board, Berlin’s twentieth. Lena had Gdańsk, a union, and both. I gave her both. Margot wrote BOTH and underlined it against her will.

response: “Thank you,” Lena says, the way you’d thank a man for passing the salt, and then, because she can’t leave it there: “Say it again slower. Margot’s spelling it.”

choices.text: “Bread doesn’t knock down walls. Seventy thousand candles did.”

journal.title: On the Wall
journal.text: On the Wall — unofficial, Margot’s board, Berlin’s twentieth. Lena had Gdańsk, a union, and both. I had Leipzig and seventy thousand candles. Costigan — candles. It’s on the board until somebody needs the board.

response: “Seventy thousand people who’d had *breakfast*,” Lena says, and somewhere in it they’ve both ended up on their feet without either of them remembering standing, and Margot has to say “Thank you” twice, at volume, before anybody sits.

choices.text: “Margot. Write down ‘both.’ Write down I said it first.”

journal.title: On the Wall
journal.text: On the Wall — unofficial, Margot’s board, Berlin’s twentieth. Lena had Gdańsk, a union, Leipzig too, and called it both. I said “both” first, as a joke. Margot says a concession with a joke in it is a concession. Broussard, on points.

response: Margot does not write it down. “A concession with a joke in it,” she says, “is a concession.”
Lena puts both arms straight up over her head like she’s just cleared the bar at a track meet. “I’ll take it,” she says. “I’ll take it from either of you.”

choices.text: “What I said about my father. That was me, not the argument.”

journal.title: On the Wall
journal.text: On the Wall — unofficial, Margot’s board, Berlin’s twentieth. Lena had Gdańsk, a union, and both. I gave her both. Margot wrote BOTH and underlined it against her will. I said something about my father that wasn’t an argument. I took it back.

response: Lena looks at him from the arm of the couch. “I know it was,” she says. “It’s all right, Jack.” And then, to Margot, before the room can make anything of it: “He means both.”

body: Margot uncaps the marker one last time and writes the decision across the bottom of the board, under all four columns, in capitals the size of a headline.

body.title: THE 4TH-FLOOR WHITEBOARD
body.text: 20 YEARS · WHO BROUGHT IT DOWN? — BROUSSARD, ON POINTS. (HE WAS WINNING. THEN HE WAS FUNNY.)

body: Theo applauds from the carpet without getting up. Laney announces that it was the most beautiful thing she has seen in this lounge since Doug ate a Hot Pocket frozen, “on a dare from *himself*.” Kevin stops the stopwatch and reads the total like a pulse. “Thirty-one minutes, forty seconds. Resting. Good job, everybody.”

body.text: Lena stops at Jack’s chair on her way to the counter, and for a second he thinks she’s going to say something about his father. She puts her hand on the back of the chair instead, just long enough to take it away again.
She takes the empty bowl out of his hands and stacks it on the lid of the stockpot to carry down. “Go to bed, Youngstown,” she says, warm. “You argue worse tired.”

She collects her cold mug off the coffee table, tips the last of it into the sink, and on the way out knocks twice on the top of Jack’s head with one knuckle. “Go to bed, Youngstown,” she says, warm. “You argue worse tired.”

body: Theo goes out ahead of him, pitching the Hasselhoff picture to the empty hallway. Margot leaves the board as it is. Kevin turns the TV off on the last of the dominoes lying flat in a street in Berlin, where it is nearly seven in the morning, and somebody — Laney, from the look of the corners — has tucked the afghan up under Doug’s chin.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 11:20 AM · THE BLUFF BENCH, SEACLIFF ROAD
body: Veterans Day comes up clear and mild, the kind of November Marisol does to people from Ohio out of spite: seventy degrees by eleven, the Channel flat and blue all the way out to the islands, the kelp lying on the water in dark rafts. Down the coast at Campus Point the flag over the Marine Lab hangs at half-staff and doesn’t stir. Across Seacliff the Pi Lam porch is empty except for a pink cowboy hat somebody left on the swing.

It’s the bench where Lena said *Hi, Danny* into his phone in September. Jack has had three hours of sleep in two nights, and he has Hector’s Wednesday shift tonight so Hector can have his Thursday. He sits with his elbows on his knees and the sun on the back of his neck and doesn’t think about anything in particular, which takes effort.
Lena comes along the bluff from the Grove end peeling an orange with her thumbnail, in the green sweatshirt and her boots, and she gets one look at him from ten yards off.

body.text: “You look like a man who argued with a whiteboard and won,” she says. “That’s worse.” She sits down beside him.
“You look like a man who argued with a whiteboard and lost,” she says, and sits down beside him.

body: He goes into the Carhartt for the Reds without deciding to.

body.text: There’s one fewer in the pack than there was on Monday night.

body: Lena doesn’t say anything. She holds out her palm.

He gives her one. The Altoids tin comes out of her boot, and she tears a strip off the back of Sunday’s St. Brendan’s bulletin, uncaps a pen with her teeth and writes on her knee in her small hard capitals, *No. 9 · the bluff bench · 11/11/09 · Veterans Day*, and shuts the cigarette in with it. “Nine,” she says. She doesn’t smoke any of it.
She splits the orange and hands him half without asking whether he wants it.

“It’s Martin of Tours today,” she says, working a seed out with her tongue. “Roman soldier. Rides up on a beggar at the gate in Amiens in the dead of winter, takes his sword to his own cloak and gives him half.” She eats a section. “Everybody forgets the beggar took it. Stood there in the snow and let a soldier give him half a coat. That’s the half nobody puts on the holy card.”

She isn’t making a point; she’s eating an orange. The flag at the Marine Lab lifts once in a breath of wind and drops again. Lena wipes her fingers on her skirt and looks at him sideways, the way she looks at a paper she’s about to mark, and waits.

choices.key: On the bluff bench you told Lena about your father’s night in the Lordstown lot.
response: So he tells her. The SUB pay that ran out last week. The bar, for the Steelers game, and the bar closing, and the truck not coming back, and his father’s cell phone on the kitchen counter. His mother at four in the morning her time, very calm. Nonna at the table with her beads. The trash can at the curb that he heard go over through the phone, two thousand miles off. And the lot at Lordstown, where his father sat in the Silverado half the night to see if the lights were on.

response.text: She lets him finish every sentence. Friday night in the Grove he had to be told to.

response: She doesn’t argue with any of it, and she doesn’t try to fix it. When he’s done she sits a while with her shoulder against his.

“Daddy didn’t drink about the storm,” she says. “He gutted houses. Ours first, down to the studs, then my uncle’s, then every neighbor on Dupre Street who’d let him in the door. Two years, with his brothers and a pry bar. Mama used to have to go get him off other people’s roofs for supper.” She looks out at the islands. “Some men drink and some men gut houses. Yours hasn’t got a house to gut, Jack.” Then, practical, the way she gives directions: “Call him Saturday. Ohio State’s playing Iowa — it’s a big one, even I know that. Don’t talk about this. Talk about that.” And, when he looks at her: “I read the sports page. I’m not a nun.”

Then, unprompted: “What I said Monday. About your daddy and who won. I’d have said it different if I’d known.” “You’d have said it.” “I’d have said it *different*.” She keeps the argument. He doesn’t want her to give it up.

response.text: He tells her about the hold too, while he’s at it: three hundred and forty dollars by five on Friday, or no spring registration, and Hale’s seminar fills by five past seven Monday morning without him. Lena thinks about it seriously. “I’ve got forty dollars,” she says, “and half a pot of court-bouillon.” He doesn’t take the forty. He laughs, though, out loud, at the sea, and it surprises him.
response.else: He tells her about the hold too, while he’s at it: three hundred and forty dollars by five on Friday, or no spring registration, and Hale’s seminar fills by five past seven Monday morning without him. Lena thinks about it seriously. “I’ve got forty dollars,” she says, “and a napkin.” He doesn’t take the forty. He laughs, though, out loud, at the sea, and it surprises him.

response: Across the Grove the Ferrer Tower chimes the three-quarters, faint and a little flat. Lena gets up, shakes the orange peel out of her skirt into one hand, and puts it in her pocket with the tin. “Twelve-ten,” she says. “Come pray for the Browns.” They go in under the eucalyptus with the sea at their backs.

choices.key: On the bluff bench you showed Lena your sister’s texts.
response: He flips the RAZR open to them and hands it over. Lena reads with her thumb on the little silver d-pad, scrolling down through Gina’s lowercase like it’s her own phone and her own sister, her mouth tight.

“Tell her the truth about that girl’s daddy isn’t hers to use,” she says. “Same as Danny isn’t that girl’s.” She scrolls on. “And tell her I’d have said it too. At fifteen I’d have said it *louder*, and in front of the nuns, and I’d have been proud of it till about Easter.”
Then she gets to the last one, the one after the gap, and her thumb stops. She reads it. She closes the phone and puts it back in his hand, warm from hers, and doesn’t ask him one thing about it.
He notices that. He sits with the RAZR shut in his fist and notices it down to the last section of orange.

The Ferrer Tower chimes the three-quarters, faint across the Grove. Lena stands and holds her hand down to him, and pulls when he takes it. “Twelve-ten,” she says. She talks about nothing, on purpose, from the bench to the church door.
“How are the evenings?” he says, and she knows which part of the evening he means.

“Nine days.” She does the arithmetic on her fingers anyway, to be sure. “I sat on the landing Monday at 8:04. Before Margot’s thing. With the phone shut, like an idiot.” She eats a section of orange. “I’m going to stop. Maybe Thursday. Thursday I’ll be somewhere loud at eight o’clock and I won’t even notice.”
“Mémère called last night,” she says, brighter, and gives him the report.

response.text: “She says you have manners. She wants it noted.”
“She lit a candle for the Browns. She says it’s the least the Church can do.”
“She wants to know who taught you to say *maigre*. She’s going to write the woman a letter.”

response: Then, looking at the islands: “You’re still coming Thursday?” “I promised.”

response.text: “Good,” Lena says. “Somebody has to sit with Laney. She’s bringing scorecards.”
“And Becca.” “On one and three.” “God love her,” Lena says, and means it.
“He’ll like that,” Lena says. “He thinks everybody leaves.”

response: The Ferrer Tower chimes the three-quarters, faint and flat across the Grove, and Lena counts the notes under her breath and stands. “Twelve-ten. You’re coming.” He is. They cut through the eucalyptus to Ocean Road with the bulletin and its missing strip folded into her pocket.
